From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe. items.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
items.excerpt: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
items.excerpt: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

items.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
items.excerpt: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

items.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
items.excerpt: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

items.title: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
items.excerpt: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view.

items.title: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
items.excerpt: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.

items.title: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
items.excerpt: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds.

items.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
items.excerpt: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

items.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
items.excerpt: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

items.excerpt: Anthropic model proves Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, PSI says Key Takeaways - • PSI says a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture in Lean - • plus new Meta Muse models, OpenAI's $11B raise and an escaped agent at WorkOS. JIUFENG Editorial November 7, 2026 24 min read PSI says a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture > Physical Superintelligence (PSI) says its internal research system used an unreleased Anthropic model to prove a quantum computing conjecture open since 2008, and that the proof passed Lean. PSI announced the result in an X thread on November 6 and published a research page the same day. PSI technical staffer David Turturean led the work. - Problem: the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008, which asks when quantum computers can beat classical machines by an exponential margin - Model: a non-public Anthropic model; the report does not name it - Verification: Lean accepted the proof on the third day of the run Limitations: The report frames the result as settling the question only "if the proof holds under outside scrutiny." Because the model is not public, nobody outside can reproduce the run. The report gives no compute or cost figures. OpenAI reportedly receives $11 billion of a new round at a $1.25 trillion valuation > Bloomberg sources say investors wired $11 billion to OpenAI on November 6, and the full round could reach about $20 billion. The round has not closed yet and is expected to close in the coming weeks. It values OpenAI at $1.25 trillion. The sources did not name the investors. OpenAI's last round was in March: $122 billion from about two dozen backers, including Microsoft, Nvidia and Amazon. ---

items.excerpt: Democrats debate possible AI rules for the next Congress Democrats are weighing AI safety tests, liability rules, child protections, and data center power costs, but they do not yet share one plan. About 2 hours ago• AI Policy & Regulation Jack Harrison In short: Democrats are discussing several different ways to regulate AI in the next Congress, but they have not agreed on a single plan. What's going on Democratic lawmakers and policy experts are floating a mix of ideas for AI rules ahead of the next Congress. The options include safety testing and audits, which are like inspections before a product goes on the market, and mandatory incident reporting, which would require companies to report serious problems when they happen. Representative Lori Trahan has supported independent expert evaluations of top AI systems and clearer legal rules for when developers can be held responsible for harm. Senator Maria Cantwell has pushed a broader framework with enforceable safety standards, ongoing testing, disclosures, and protections for children and workers. Representatives Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer are also working on a framework that would set minimum safety standards and allow government action if an AI system fails tests. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has backed the idea of a separate federal agency to oversee AI companies and during his campaign he called for a pause on “frontier AI,” meaning the most powerful new models being built. Outside government, Spencer Amdur and Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law and AI expect hearings to cover issues like hacking, cyberattacks, and child safety. An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week. In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation. The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats. Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." items.title: Nothing can be fully transparent, physicists discover
items.excerpt: Nothing can be fully transparent, physicists discover Scientific American November 7, 2026 Nothing can be fully transparent, physicists discover Quantum researchers show how materials inevitably absorb light By Matthew von Hippel edited by Clara Moskowitz His work and other recent advances might suggest that researchers are on a path toward developing a completely transparent substance. That dream was recently proved false, however, when a group of theoretical physicists found that no light-bending material can ever be fully transparent, owing to a quantum process that turns waves of light into waves of sound. The researchers argue that even the cleverest engineering will never be able to create a material that doesn’t lose some of the light that passes through it. But the loss can be very, very small. To do even better, you might turn to a stranger substance. Cool helium down to only a few degrees above absolute zero, and it becomes a kind of liquid known as a superfluid. In a superfluid, quantum mechanics coordinates the way different atoms move, letting the liquid flow with no friction at all. Liquid helium, in particular, is astonishingly clear, and although it absorbs x-rays, scientists have not been able to measure an effect on visible light. ---

items.excerpt: AI Maps Nearly 2,900 Hidden Partnerships Inside Human Mitochondria AI · BIOMEDICINE November 5 institutional release; original paper August 25, 2026 Inside every cell, mitochondria do far more than generate energy. They help manage metabolism, stress signals and essential chemical reactions. Yet scientists still cannot explain what hundreds of mitochondrial proteins actually do. That missing knowledge makes it harder to connect genetic mutations to disease. Researchers at Texas A&M AgriLife have now used artificial intelligence to assemble a much more detailed map of potential partnerships among these proteins. The team used AlphaFold-Multimer to examine 630,003 possible pairings among roughly 1,100 proteins. It identified 2,895 likely interactions, more than half not previously reported. For 85 poorly characterized proteins, the predictions offered possible interaction partners for the first time. Such partners can provide clues: if an unknown protein repeatedly binds proteins involved in copper handling, for example, it may participate in the same cellular pathway. Crucially, this was not simply a computer-generated list. The researchers spent roughly two years testing selected predictions in yeast and human cells, confirming several of the proposed interactions. They also released a resource called MitoMatch so other laboratories can prioritize experiments rather than screening every combination from scratch. The distinction between prediction and discovery matters. Most proposed pairs have not been experimentally verified, and a predicted interaction does not establish its physiological importance. The paper itself first appeared on August 25; the November 5 university announcement is the new event here. No medicine or diagnostic test follows directly from this work. items.excerpt: How Femtosecond X-Rays Solved Chemistry's Contentious Molecular Switch Mystery (2026) Femtosecond X-rays Solve Controverse Over How Azobenzene Flips Between Isomers Firing femtosecond x-ray pulses at azobenzene has helped chemists study how its structure changes as it flips between isomers in solution, finding that a twisting of the carbon–nitrogen bond initiates the reaction. The researchers behind the work say that this is the first time that their technique has been used on molecules made up of only lighter atoms. The team also suggests that their technique could be used to study other fast, light-driven reactions. Using time-resolved x-ray liquidography, the team excited azobenzene with an ultraviolet laser and fired femtosecond x-ray pulses at the molecule at different time points. By analyzing the scattered x-rays, they were able to determine the distance between atoms and build up a picture of the molecule’s structure. They found that the reaction does not begin with a twist around the central N=N double bond, but instead with a pedal-like motion of the azo group, changing the angle between the phenyl rings and the azo group. While the technique has previously only worked for molecules containing heavy atoms, the team believes it could be used to study other fast, light-driven reactions, including proton-transfer reactions, ring openings, and photoactive proteins. They are now hoping to use the technique to see how chemical modifications to photoswitches like azobenzene change its motion from one isomer to another. Last Updated: 2026-11-07T20:05:18+07:00

items.excerpt: Guinea-Bissau Cancels US-Funded Hepatitis B Vaccine Trial on Newborns Guinea-Bissau's health authorities have cancelled a planned hepatitis B vaccine trial on newborn babies after international critics called the US-funded study unethical and exploitative. Key points WHAT HAPPENED - Guinea-Bissau has cancelled a planned hepatitis B vaccine trial - Only half of enrolled newborns would have received the vaccine - US research partners were set to fund the cancelled study AllAfrica· November 7, 2026 at 4:36 AM· 13 h ago Guinea-Bissau's health ministry has cancelled a planned trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies after the study drew sharp international criticism over its design. The trial, which was to be funded through US research partners, would have given the vaccine to only half of the enrolled infants, leaving the rest unprotected as a comparison group. Public health advocates and local officials argued the design was unethical, noting that an effective hepatitis B vaccine is already widely available and routinely given to newborns in wealthier countries. Critics said withholding it from half the infants amounted to a form of testing that would likely not be approved in the nations funding the research. Authorities in Guinea-Bissau said the trial will not proceed in its current form and signalled that any future studies involving the country's children will face stricter ethical review. The decision adds to a wider debate across West Africa over how foreign-funded clinical research is designed, approved and overseen. ---
